bib.title: AnyTool: Self-Reflective, Hierarchical Agents for Large-Scale API Calls

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "AnyTool: Self-Reflective, Hierarchical Agents for Large-Scale API Calls", Yu Du, Fangyun Wei, Hongyang Zhang (Tsinghua, Microsoft Research Asia, Waterloo). The PDF is arXiv:2402.04253v1, 6 Feb 2024, and prints no venue, so treat it as a preprint. Year: 2024.

COVERAGE: All 17 pages and all 68,591 chars were read, including the appendices (Tables 8-21, case study). Figures 1-7 are charts or diagrams whose values did not extract. Only the text and table values are reported.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Claim: A hierarchical GPT-4 retriever (meta-agent, category agents, tool agents) plus a solver and self-reflection loop reaches 58.2% average pass rate on filtered ToolBench, against 22.9% for ToolLLM's original pipeline.
  number: 58.2 vs 22.9 (Table 1 Avg.)
  setup: Filtered ToolBench (G1-I/T/C, G2-I/C, G3-I), 16K+ RapidAPI APIs, GPT-4 function calling, DFSDT solver, pass rate by Eq 2, GPT-4-32K judge. Results are reproduced by the authors.
  quote: "AnyTool (Ours) SR Agent SR GPT-4 w/ DFSDT 52.2 61.4 67.6 58.9 45.9 63.2 58.2" and "ToolLLM ToolLLM’s ToolLLaMA w/ DFSDT 28.4 26.3 38.4 21.5 15.1 7.7 22.9"
  where: p.6, Table 1
- Claim: AnyTool beats GPT-4 given the reference (gold) APIs. The text reports +32.6 over ToolLLM and +19.3 over GPT-4 with reference APIs, while the abstract says +35.4%.
  number: 58.2 vs 38.9 (+19.3)
  setup: The baselines get the benchmark's reference APIs, so no retrieval is needed. AnyTool searches all 16K+.
  quote: "significantly outperforms both the original ToolLLM and GPT-4 using reference APIs, by +32.6 and +19.3 points, respectively, in terms of the average pass rate." Abstract: "AnyTool outperforms ToolLLM by +35.4% in terms of average pass rate on ToolBench."
  where: p.1 abstract; p.7. The +32.6 matches the 25.6 row (ToolLLaMA with reference APIs, 58.2-25.6). The abstract's +35.4 does not match the 22.9 row, which gives 35.3. The paper is inconsistent here.
- Claim: A plain GPT-4 agent (14.0%) and AutoGen-RAG with embeddings (13.1%) retrieve far worse than the hierarchy over the same pool.
  number: 15.2 (plain agent) and 13.1 (AutoGen-RAG) vs 58.2 avg
  setup: Table 1. The plain agent sees 500 APIs per group (33 groups). AutoGen-RAG uses 1,000-token chunks.
  quote: "GPT-4 Plain Agent GPT-4 w/ DFSDT 13.9 23.5 17.6 13.9 9.2 13.2 15.2"
  where: p.6; Appendix A.4-A.5
- Claim: On the new AnyToolBench (400 queries, no reference APIs), AnyTool scores 73.8%, ToolLLM with a GPT-4 solver 36.6%, and the GPT-4 plain agent 14.0%.
  number: 73.8 / 36.6 / 18.9 / 14.0
  quote: "AnyTool (Ours) SR Agent SR GPT-4 73.8"
  where: p.7, Table 2
- Claim: Ablating the hierarchy or the self-reflection each cuts the pass rate sharply.
  number: G2-I 58.9 to 22.4 (flat) or 19.6 (no reflection). G3-I 63.2 to 15.8 for both.
  setup: Filtered ToolBench G2-I and G3-I. The flat variant merges category and tool functions into the meta-agent's function list.
  quote: "-Hierarchical Structure 22.4 15.8 / -Self-Reflection 19.6 15.8 / -DFSDT/+CoT 50.5 60.3"
  where: p.7, Table 3. Swapping DFSDT for CoT costs 8.4 and 2.9 points.
- Claim: Self-reflection re-activates agents bottom-up (tool, then category, then meta). Re-activating more levels gives higher pass rates.
  number: G2-I/G3-I 43.9/44.7 (tool agents only), 55.2/55.3 (+category), 58.9/63.2 (all)
  quote: "Tool Agents 43.9 44.7 / Tool Agents + Category Agents 55.2 55.3 / All Agents 58.9 63.2"
  where: p.7, Table 4
- Claim: Pass rate rises with extra reflection rounds, by up to 20% in 4-6 iterations.
  number: up to 20% (stated in prose; Fig 3 values not extractable)
  quote: "With only 4-6 self-reflection iterations, the pass rate improves by up to 20% across all datasets."
  where: p.2-3
- Claim: The ToolLLM pass-rate metric is inflated, because unsolvable queries count as passed.
  number: 99.0% pass rate with random API candidates
  setup: Random candidates per query, judged under the Eq 1 protocol. Eq 1 counts #(Non-solvable) in the numerator.
  quote: "when API candidates are randomly selected for each query, GPT-4 predominantly labels them as “non-solvable”, resulting in an inflated pass rate of 99.0% through the metric defined in Eq 1."
  where: p.4. The authors' fix is Eq 2, Solved/(Solved+Unsolved), plus a manual filter of ToolBench to solvable queries.
- Claim: The GPT-4 judge agrees with humans far better than GPT-3.5 does.
  number: 96.5% vs 73.9%
  setup: G1-I subset, AnyTool solutions.
  quote: "GPT-4’s alignment with human evaluation stands at 96.5%, while that of GPT-3.5 is only 73.9%."
  where: p.6
- Claim: A bigger searchable API pool gives a higher pass rate.
  number: G2-I/G3-I 18.6/7.9 (1K), 26.3/23.7 (5K), 38.1/36.8 (10K), 58.9/63.2 (all)
  setup: Random subsets of the pool.
  where: p.8, Table 5
- Claim: Candidate-pool cap and tools per tool agent show saturation or trade-offs.
  number: Pool cap 16/32/64 gives G2-I 49.5/58.9/58.9 and G3-I 42.1/55.3/63.2. Tools per tool agent K=3/5/10 gives G2-I 48.6/58.9/52.3 and G3-I 42.1/57.9/39.5.
  quote: "managing too many tools (e.g., K = 10) leads to a larger search space and may cause overlooking of relevant APIs, while managing too few tools (e.g., K = 3) might result in lower recall."
  where: p.8, Tables 6-7
- Claim: Cost is high, at about 135K tokens and 43 OpenAI calls per query.
  number: 13.5 × 10^4 tokens, 14.1 API candidates, 43.3 calls, 4.6 self-reflections per query on average
  setup: Averaged across all datasets. A 200,000-token cap per query and at most 10 API calls in the DFSDT solver.
  quote: "each query consumes 13.5 × 104 tokens, identifies 14.1 API candidates, and involves 43.3 OpenAI API calls and 4.6 self-reflections."
  where: p.12, A.6; p.11, A.1
- Claim: Giving the plain agent more information (names, descriptions, details) barely helps, and the embedding model barely matters for RAG.
  number: Plain agent G2-I 13.1 / 15.9 / 13.1, G3-I 13.2 throughout. RAG G2-I 8.4 (ada-002) vs 7.4 (mpnet).
  where: p.12, Tables 10-11
- Claim: On the original, unfiltered ToolBench, AnyTool averages 44.8 against ToolLLM's 20.4 (ToolLLaMA) and 32.2 (GPT-4 solver).
  quote: "AnyTool (Ours) SR Agent SR GPT-4 w/ DFSDT 46.0 54.0 53.0 37.0 46.5 32.0 44.8"
  where: p.11, Table 9. All queries are counted, solvable or not, under Eq 2.
- Claim: Design mechanics worth noting.
  - The solver's "finish" returns Give Solution, Try Backtrack, or Give Up. On Give Up it must name the irrelevant or failed APIs, which are pruned from the pool and history before the retry.
  - Reflection triggers when GPT-4 judges a proposed solution as not solving the query, or when the solver gives up.
  - Agents that called finish_search are not re-activated.
  - Retriever agents run multi-threaded, each with its own history. All stop when a tool agent's check_if_request_solvable returns True.
  where: pp.4-6

LIMITS
- Authors concede (Impact Statements): "its performance in extremely complex scenarios has not been verified, owing to the absence of appropriate datasets." They also note the dependence on GPT-4's function calling.
- Authors concede wall-clock time was not measured: "calculating the processing time ... is infeasible" because the GPT-4 server response is unstable.
- The judge is GPT-4 only, validated on G1-I only (96.5% agreement).
- Filtered ToolBench subsets are small, at 115, 132, 142, 107, 98 and 38 queries. G3-I has 38, so differences there are noisy.
- The authors filtered the benchmark and built AnyToolBench themselves. GPT-4 generated its queries and reference solutions, so the benchmark could favor GPT-4-based agents.
- The baselines are weak by construction. The ToolLLM retriever is a trained model. The plain and RAG GPT-4 baselines were implemented by the authors, and the plain agent scans in groups.
- The paper's "self-reflection" is closer to feedback-driven re-search than a verified-correction loop. It cites Huang et al. 2023 (LLMs cannot self-correct reasoning) as a negative result, but does not test it directly.
- It is dated: it uses GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 function calling from 2023, RapidAPI tools, and the DFSDT/ToolBench setup. There is no MCP, no long-context retrieval comparison, and no sampling variance or seeds reported.
- The Table 3 ablation uses one run each, with no intervals.

BUILDS ON: ToolLLM / ToolBench (Qin et al. 2023b: dual-phase retrieve-then-solve, DFSDT, evaluation protocol, 16K RapidAPI APIs); GPT-4 function calling (Achiam et al. 2023); Chain of Thought (Wei et al. 2022); AutoGen RAG baseline, cited as Augenstein et al. 2023 (the paper's own citation looks wrong); self-reflection literature: RAIN (Li et al. 2024), self-play (Chen et al. 2024), self-rewarding LMs (Yuan et al. 2024), Self-Instruct (Wang et al. 2022), Huang et al. 2023. Related tool work cited: Toolformer (Schick et al. 2023), Gorilla (Patil et al. 2023), API-Bank (Li et al. 2023), HuggingGPT (Shen et al. 2023), RestGPT, ToolAlpaca, TALM. ReAct is not cited.

CODE: No code is included. The paper says only "Code will be available at https://github.com/dyabel/AnyTool." Verbatim prompts are available (Tables 14-20). The re-activation prompt for tool agents, Table 18 (p.15):
"The current APIs have failed to solve the query, resulting in: {fail reason}. You need to analyze this result and seek additional APIs. It’s possible that the tools lack the relevant APIs. In such cases, you should call the Finish function. Remember not to invent tool or API names."
The Table 8 function lists, per agent type, are on p.11.

FIGURES (not extracted by the figures script; captions are from the text)
- Fig 2, p.2: overview of the meta-agent / category agent / tool agent hierarchy, the function list per agent, and the solver and self-reflection loop. It is the fastest way to see the architecture.
- Fig 3, p.2: pass rate versus number of self-reflection rounds per dataset.
- Fig 4, p.4: the ToolLLM evaluation protocol (a) versus the revised one (b). It shows the metric flaw.
- Figs 5-6, p.8: average self-reflection frequency and agent count per dataset.
- Fig 7, p.17: a case study with step-by-step retrieval, a first failure ("due to the query limit, I couldn't generate a random word"), reflection, and a corrected answer.

PROBLEMS: No extraction faults beyond garbled equations (Eq 1 and Eq 2 are flattened) and chart-only data. There were no embedded instructions. The abstract's +35.4% does not match the body's +32.6 and +19.3. The paper does not name the venue, and I did not infer one. Page-level offsets were not tracked, so locations are page numbers from the PDF pages.
